title: What is CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) — attacker tricks a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted request to your server — and how to prevent it (CSRF token in forms, SameSite cookie attribute)?
shortTitle: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) and How to Prevent It

s1_definition.profdef: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is an attack that tricks a victim's browser into sending an unwanted, state-changing request to a site where the victim is already authenticated, abusing the browser's habit of automatically attaching cookies. Because the forged request carries the victim's valid session cookie, the server believes it is legitimate. The standard defenses are an anti-CSRF token (a secret, per-session value the attacker cannot read or guess, required on state-changing requests) and the SameSite cookie attribute, which stops the browser from sending the cookie on cross-site requests.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh is logged into National Bank of India in one tab. In another tab he visits a malicious site that secretly contains a hidden form which auto-submits a transfer request to the bank. Because the browser automatically attaches Rajesh's bank cookie, the bank sees a seemingly valid "transfer 50000 to the attacker" instruction and obeys it. A CSRF token is like the bank requiring a secret one-time stamp that only its own genuine pages print; the malicious site cannot know the stamp, so its forged instruction is rejected.
s1_definition.oneliner: CSRF rides the victim's auto-sent cookie; stop it with an unguessable token and SameSite cookies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is an attack that tricks a victim's browser into sending an unwanted, state-changing request to a site where the victim is already authenticated, abusing the browser's habit of automatically attaching cookies. Because the forged request carries the victim's valid session cookie, the server believes it is legitimate. The standard defenses are an anti-CSRF token (a secret, per-session value the attacker cannot read or guess, required on state-changing requests) and the SameSite cookie attribute, which stops the browser from sending the cookie on cross-site requests.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh is logged into National Bank of India in one tab. In another tab he visits a malicious site that secretly contains a hidden form which auto-submits a transfer request to the bank. Because the browser automatically attaches Rajesh's bank cookie, the bank sees a seemingly valid "transfer 50000 to the attacker" instruction and obeys it. A CSRF token is like the bank requiring a secret one-time stamp that only its own genuine pages print; the malicious site cannot know the stamp, so its forged instruction is rejected.

**One line to remember:** CSRF rides the victim's auto-sent cookie; stop it with an unguessable token and SameSite cookies.

sections.s2_technical:
CSRF works because browsers automatically attach cookies to any request to a domain, regardless of which site initiated it. An attacker's page can auto-submit a form or fire an image/script request to `POST /transfer`, and the victim's cookie goes along. The attacker never reads the response; the damage is the side effect — money moved, email changed. It targets state-changing requests, so safe idempotent GETs should not change state.

The main defense is the synchronizer token pattern: the server embeds a random anti-CSRF token in each form or sends it in a header, and requires it on every state-changing request. The attacker's cross-site page cannot read this token (same-origin policy blocks reading the victim's pages), so it cannot include it, and the request is rejected. In Spring Security, CSRF protection is on by default for session-based apps; the token is exposed to the front end (for SPAs) via a cookie like `XSRF-TOKEN` and echoed in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header.

The second defense is the SameSite cookie attribute: `Set-Cookie: session=...; SameSite=Strict` (or Lax) tells the browser not to attach the cookie on cross-site requests, which neutralizes most CSRF at the browser level. The senior nuances: token-based APIs that send credentials in the Authorization header (not cookies) are not CSRF-prone, because the browser does not auto-attach headers; CSRF matters specifically for cookie-based auth. Combine SameSite with CSRF tokens for defense in depth, and never rely on checking only the Referer/Origin header, though verifying Origin is a useful additional signal.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh is logged into National Bank of India. A malicious page he visits auto-submits a transfer to the attacker's account, and the browser attaches Rajesh's session cookie, so the bank almost executes it. This is exactly CSRF — a forged request riding the victim's cookie.

Problem 2 — The bank must distinguish requests that genuinely came from its own pages from forged cross-site ones. This is exactly what the anti-CSRF token does — only the bank's real pages carry the secret token, which the attacker cannot read.

Our mini-project builds a `CsrfProtectedTransferService` that requires a valid per-session CSRF token on transfers, plus a `SameSiteCookie` helper. The demo shows a legitimate transfer with the correct token succeeding, a forged transfer without the token being rejected, and SameSite=Strict refusing to send the cookie cross-site.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run
javac CsrfDefenseDemo.java
java com.bank.csrf.CsrfDefenseDemo

# Spring Boot (CSRF on by default for session apps)
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/csrf-defense-service-1.0.0.jar

# A transfer without the X-XSRF-TOKEN header is rejected
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers -b 'SESSION=abc' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CUR3001","amount":50000}'   # 403 without token
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a session for Rajesh, a legitimate transfer carrying the correct CSRF token, and a forged transfer without it.

Step 1: The bank's genuine page gets a CSRF token issued and bound to Rajesh's session. Only pages served by the bank carry this token.

Step 2: The legitimate transfer presents the correct token. The service compares it to the expected token for the session, they match, and the transfer proceeds.

Step 3: A malicious site auto-submits a forged transfer. The browser attaches Rajesh's session cookie automatically, but the attacker's page cannot read the bank's token, so it presents a missing or guessed value. The service finds the token does not match and throws, rejecting the forged request — the CSRF attack fails.

Step 4: Independently, with SameSite=Strict the browser would not even attach the session cookie to the cross-site request, so the forged request would arrive unauthenticated. The two defenses together — token mismatch rejection and SameSite blocking — give layered protection.

```text
2026-10-31 23:45:00.010 INFO    [CsrfDefenseDemo] Bank page holds CSRF token for the session
2026-10-31 23:45:00.012 INFO    [CsrfDefenseDemo] Legitimate transfer accepted (valid CSRF token)
2026-10-31 23:45:00.013 SEVERE  [CsrfDefenseDemo] Forged (CSRF) transfer rejected: missing or invalid CSRF token
2026-10-31 23:45:00.014 INFO    [CsrfDefenseDemo] Cookie sent on cross-site request (SameSite=Strict)? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Rajesh logged into bank (session cookie set)
    │
    ├─ LEGIT PATH (bank's own page)        ├─ ATTACK PATH (evil site auto-submit)
    │  form has CSRF token T               │  no access to token T
    │  POST /transfer + cookie + T         │  POST /transfer + cookie (auto) only
    │  server: T == expected ✓             │  server: token missing/mismatch ✗
    ▼                                       ▼

  SameSite=Strict: cross-site request does NOT even carry the cookie
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cross-Site Request Forgery, or CSRF, is an attack that tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted, state-changing request to a site where the user is already authenticated. It works because browsers automatically attach cookies to any request to a domain, so a forged request from a malicious page carries the victim's valid session cookie and the server believes it is genuine. The attacker never needs to read the response; the harm is the side effect, like a transfer or a changed email.

In my banking project the scenario is Rajesh logged into National Bank of India in one tab while a malicious page in another tab auto-submits a transfer to the attacker. Because the browser attaches his session cookie, the bank would almost execute it. The defense I rely on first is the synchronizer token pattern: the bank embeds an unguessable anti-CSRF token in its own pages and requires it on every state-changing request. The attacker's cross-site page cannot read that token because the same-origin policy blocks it, so the forged request is rejected.

The second defense is the SameSite cookie attribute set to Strict or Lax, which tells the browser not to attach the session cookie on cross-site requests at all, neutralizing most CSRF at the browser level. In my demo a legitimate transfer with the correct token succeeds, a forged transfer without the token is rejected, and SameSite=Strict refuses to send the cookie cross-site. I combine both for defense in depth.

The nuance I always add is that CSRF specifically affects cookie-based authentication. APIs that send credentials in the Authorization header with a bearer token are not CSRF-prone, because the browser does not automatically attach custom headers. So in Spring Security I keep CSRF protection on for session-based apps, expose the token to SPAs via the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and X-XSRF-TOKEN header, and keep GET requests free of side effects.
